definition: Especially suitable and relevant to the situation or subject at hand.
example: The doctor offered an apposite analogy, comparing the clogged artery to a kinked garden hose.
nuance: Apposite is more formal than apt and stresses close relevance; do not confuse it with opposite, which means facing or contrary.
prompt: A student is choosing a quotation to open her essay about a long drought.
options: She opened with an apposite line from a farmer's diary describing the cracked, empty fields.
Her quotation was apposite to her thesis, arguing the reverse of everything she claimed.
She chose an apposite quotation about holiday shopping that had no link to drought.
She picked an apposite quotation simply because it was the shortest one in the book.
reasons: A quotation about parched fields bears directly on an essay about drought.
This confuses the word with opposite; a contradictory quotation is not well suited to the essay.
A quotation with no connection to the topic is the reverse of fitting.
Brevity says nothing about relevance; the word concerns how well something fits the subject.

practice.prompt: A teacher gives a short toast at a retirement party for the school librarian.
options: The guests stood in apposite rows, facing each other across the crowded room.
His apposite toast lasted forty minutes and wandered through every topic he could think of.
His apposite joke about overdue books made the retiring librarian laugh.
His apposite remark was about a movie that none of the guests had ever seen.
reasons: This mistakes the word for opposite; it does not describe physical position.
A rambling speech that drifts off subject lacks the focus and fitness the word implies.
A joke about library life suits a toast for a librarian perfectly.
A comment unrelated to the guest of honor or the audience is not suitable to the moment.
